newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Racist words pepper HK life, snobbery's the salt.
newsitem.headline: Racist words pepper HK life, snobbery's the salt.

text.p: Cantonese, the Chinese dialect spoken in Hong Kong, has a vast demeaning vocabulary for foreigners.
But people don't mean it, according to the government.

"Racial discrimination is not a significant problem in Hong Kong...colloquial expressions referring to certain races are not due to racial discrimination but merely reflect cultural differences or factors unrelated to race," said an official.
Chinese prejudices are many and varied.

Many Hong Kong citizens, who are much richer than their mainland counterparts, have until now -- less than 10 days before China regains control of the territory -- been less than humble towards their mainland counterparts.

A "Dai Lok Lo", or "mainland man", is often quietly despised for his primness. The women from north China who have flooded Hong Kong's night clubs are jeeringly referred to as "Buk Goo Gai", which is the name of a popular chicken and mushroom dish but which can also mean "northern prostitute".
"Most Hong Kong people look down on mainlanders, they make us feel cheap," said Guo Zhihui, who has worked in the territory for almost two years as a translator.

Yet, of 238 submissions to a recent consultation by the government's Home Affairs Branch, 197 said legislation against racism was unnecessary or undesirable. Only 19, or eight per cent, expressed the need to outlaw discrimination.

"I can't wait to go back to the Philippines, where people treat me as an equal," said a Filipina who has worked as a house maid in the city for a year. She and thousands of others, many of them university graduates, are commonly dubbed "Bun Mui", the equivalent of "Flip girls".
Some say that discrimination only occurs in isolated cases.
"In general, we are quite happy about the way our nationals are treated," Counsul General of the Philippines Estrella Berenguel said.
Other derogatory phrases frequently pop up on television shows and films, although the time-honoured term for Europeans -- "Gweilo" or white ghost -- has lost its original malice.
It follows that blacks are "black ghosts".
"But when compared to other countries I've been to, racism is virtually not a problem in Hong Kong," Botswana's Consul General Motlhware James Masisi said.
Young Chinese who are educated in the west are not spared either. They're called "bananas", yellow on the outside but white at heart.
Japanese are often called "Ga Tzai", mocking their way of speaking, while Indians are "Molocha", meaning devils.
